column2: Which object fits a reusable, parameterless report query that must act as a table source?
column3:
A view.
Reports can select from the same view in their FROM clauses instead of repeating its joins and filters. A view needs no input parameters.
Review source

column2: Which SQL object lets reports use a SELECT in FROM while exposing only chosen employee columns?
column3:
A view.
Expose only columns such as EmployeeID and Name. Give the reporting role access to the view without granting a separate path to the SSN column.
Review source

column2: A base column is renamed. How can its view keep existing reports working?
column3:
Preserve a stable set of output columns while adapting the view definition.
If a base column moves or changes name, update the view to expose the name and type callers expect. The view does not adapt automatically.
Review source

column2: What can let a view support one modification that changes several base tables?
column3:
An INSTEAD OF trigger.
The trigger handles the write in place of the ordinary view operation. For example, it can take a submitted row and write the appropriate fields to two base tables.
CREATE TRIGGER dbo.UpdateCustomerName
ON dbo.CustomerNames
INSTEAD OF UPDATE
AS
BEGIN
    UPDATE c SET CustomerName = i.CustomerName
    FROM dbo.Customers AS c
    JOIN inserted AS i ON i.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;
END;
Review source

column2: How do you grant read-only access to a reporting role when the view itself allows updates?
column3:
SELECT access without effective data-modification permissions.
Grant SELECT on the view and make sure no other permission grants that role a write path. Hiding columns does not make the remaining columns read-only.
GRANT SELECT ON OBJECT::dbo.ActiveCustomers TO ReportUser;
Review source

column2: Which object fits an explicitly called order workflow with several data changes in one transaction?
column3:
A stored procedure.
The caller can explicitly start the workflow, and the procedure can commit its changes together or roll them back on failure. The procedure does not provide atomicity on its own.
Review source

column2: Which object can return several named OUTPUT parameter values to its caller?
column3:
A stored procedure.
For example, one call can fill separate variables for the order subtotal and tax. An integer RETURN status code is separate from those values.
Review source

column2: Which SQL object can a client call to save an order and receive its details as a result set?
column3:
A stored procedure.
The procedure can save an order and then SELECT its new details for the client. A normal procedure call cannot go directly in a FROM clause.
Review source

column2: Which object fits a shipping-cost calculation reused directly in a SELECT expression?
column3:
A scalar user-defined function.
For example, the query can call the function with each shipment's weight and zone. The returned amount is a single value that fits in the SELECT list.
Review source

column2: Which object returns parameterized customer orders that another query can use in a JOIN?
column3:
A table-valued function.
Pass the customer ID to the function, then join its returned rows to another source. An ordinary view cannot take that ID as an input parameter.
Review source

column2: Which TVF type fits reusable parameterized logic expressible as a single SELECT query?
column3:
An inline table-valued function.
The one SELECT defines the table result. SQL Server can optimize the function's query and the caller's query together.
Review source

column2: What kind of TVF lets you populate a named return table in several steps?
column3:
A multi-statement table-valued function.
The function declares the result columns and can use multiple statements to fill its local return table. This is supported in Fabric SQL database, not Fabric Warehouse.
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column2: Which object can automatically record Salary changes when UPDATE statements modify an employee table?
column3:
A DML trigger.
A DML trigger runs for the UPDATE statement and can compare inserted with deleted. Comparing both versions distinguishes actual salary changes from assignments of the same value.
Review source

column2: Before writing a trigger to reject invalid data, what simpler database option should you consider?
column3:
Whether a suitable declarative constraint can enforce the rule.
A CHECK constraint can enforce a simple rule such as Quantity being positive. Prefer an appropriate constraint before adding code that runs automatically on each write.
Review source

column2: An application decides when to run a database workflow. Why make it a procedure rather than a trigger?
column3:
An explicit call makes the workflow and its effects easier to trace.
Application code can show exactly when it calls the procedure. A trigger instead runs as a side effect of the configured database event.
Review source

column2: What happens to the original modification if its DML trigger rolls back the transaction?
column3:
The original modification is rolled back too.
A rollback reverses both the trigger's changes and the triggering write. The trigger does not commit its work separately.
Review source

column2: Why can a WHERE filter that calls a non-inlined scalar UDF be slow on a large table?
column3:
Repeated calls can add per-row execution overhead.
Calling a separate function for many rows can add work that the plan cannot optimize across calls. Inspect the actual plan before replacing the function.
Review source

column2: Which SQL Server 2019-and-later feature exposes eligible T-SQL scalar UDF logic within the calling query plan?
column3:
Scalar UDF inlining.
Inlining replaces eligible calls with expressions or subqueries the optimizer can see. It requires compatibility level 150 or higher, and the function and call must qualify.
Review source

column2: Which SQL Server 2017-and-later feature improves row-count estimates for eligible multi-statement TVF queries?
column3:
Interleaved execution.
SQL Server can execute an eligible function during optimization to learn its actual row count. At compatibility level 140 or higher, that count can inform later join choices.
Review source

column2: If SQL Server caches a plan for a query that uses a nonindexed view, what does that plan cover?
column3:
The combined plan for the query and expanded view.
The optimizer expands a nonindexed view into the caller's query. The resulting plan can be cached, but the view does not get a separate plan.
Review source

column2: Why keep view definitions focused rather than deeply nesting views?
column3:
Deep layers can complicate maintenance and query optimization.
A chain of views can hide joins and filters from the person reading the top-level query. Extra layers do not cache intermediate results or guarantee a faster plan.
Review source

column2: What property must a function have to give an indexed view repeatable results for the same inputs and database state?
column3:
Determinism.
The same inputs and database state must yield the same result. An indexed view also requires the function to be schema-bound and to avoid data and external access.
Review source

column2: Why avoid sending application results from a DML trigger instead of from an explicit query?
column3:
Trigger result sets are discouraged and can break calling applications.
A result set from a trigger can reach a caller that expects only the original write response. Return application data from an explicit query or procedure instead.
Review source

column2: Why choose a stored procedure over a T-SQL UDF for logic that directly updates permanent tables?
column3:
User-defined functions cannot directly modify permanent database state.
A T-SQL UDF can compute a value or fill a local return table, but it cannot write to an application table. A procedure can perform that write.
Review source
